'''''Fittonia albivenis''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Acanthaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to the rainforests of Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and northern Brazil. An [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], it is notable for its dark green foliage with strongly contrasting white or red veins. It is commonly called '''nerve plant''' or '''mosaic plant'''. In [[temperateness|temperate]] regions where the temperature falls below {{convert|10|C|F|abbr=on}} it must be grown as a [[houseplant]].<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image: Fittonia_albivenis_002.JPG|thumb|left|Inflorescence|180px]]
[[File:FittoniaAlbivenisFainted.jpg|thumb|A "fainted" or dried-out ''Fittonia albivenis''. Though it appears dead, it will revive back to a normal state after being watered.]]
''Fittonia albivenis'' is a creeping evergreen perennial growing to {{convert|15|cm|0|abbr=on}} high, with lush green, [[Glossary of botanical terms#ovate|ovate]] leaves, 7 to 10 cm long, with accented veins of white to deep pink and a short fuzz covering its stems. Flowers are small with a white to off-white color.<ref>Rob Herwig: Parey's Houseplant Encyclopedia . Edited by Richard Maatsch. Parey, Berlin / Hamburg 1983. {{ISBN|3-489-61024-5}}</ref>
[[File:Fittonia albivenis leaf detail.jpg|thumb|Leaf detail, showing the prominent white veins]]

==Cultivation==
The species is used as an [[ornamental plant]] that requires fertile soils or substrates based on [[peat]].<ref name="ars"/> It is best kept in a moist area with mild sunlight, although it does not demand much light, and temperatures above {{convert|55|F|C}}. As such, in temperate locations it must be kept under glass as a [[houseplant]].{{Cn|date=May 2021}}

It must be watered regularly. Without water for a few days, it is known to "faint" but is easily revived with a quick watering and resumes its healthiness. ''Fittonia albivenis'' is known to be hard to grow, so it is best bought at a nursery then cared for. Its spreading habit makes it ideal as [[groundcover]].{{Cn|date=May 2021}}

Numerous [[cultivars]] have been selected, falling into two cultivar groups, the Argyroneura Group (formerly ''F. argyroneura'', ''F. verschaffeltii'' var. ''argyroneura'') with silver to white veins,<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Fittonia albivenis'' Argyroneura Group|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/84077/Fittonia-albivenis-Argyroneura-Group/Details|accessdate=4 July 2020|archive-date=4 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704143046/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/84077/Fittonia-albivenis-Argyroneura-Group/Details|url-status=live}}</ref> and the Verschaffeltii Group (formerly F. verschaffeltii) with pink to red veins,<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/77753/Fittonia-albivenis-Verschaffeltii-Group/Details| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Fittonia albivensis'' Verschaffeltii Group| accessdate = 27 February 2018| archive-date = 5 July 2020| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200705051402/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/77753/Fittonia-albivenis-Verschaffeltii-Group/Details| url-status = live}}</ref> both of which have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 39 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 27 February 2018 | archive-date = 5 January 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180105180412/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Kofan people|Kofan]], [[Siona people|Siona]] and [[Secoya]] tribes of the [[Ecuador|Ecuadorian Amazon]] use ''F. albivenis'' as a treatment for headaches,<ref name="manu">{{cite web |url=http://manu.montana.com/plants.html |title=Plants |publisher=manu.montana.com |accessdate=2008-02-25 |last= |first= |archive-date=2020-11-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111231257/http://manu.montana.com/plants.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and muscular pain, its leaves were used by the [[Machiguenga]] as a [[hallucinogen]] before they were introduced to ''[[Psychotria viridis]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bioetica.org/umsa/biblioteca/russo.htm |title=Headache treatments by native peoples of the Ecuadorian Amazon |publisher=Universidad del Museo Social Argentino |accessdate=2013-05-19 |last=Russo |first=Ethan B. |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130616090824/http://www.bioetica.org/umsa/biblioteca/russo.htm |archive-date=2013-06-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> They are said to "produce visions of eyeballs." The leaves of this species are prepared as a tea in the northwestern part of the Amazon region and used for [[toothache]].<ref name="manu"/>
